ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT Article history: Background: Laboratory test results are critical to clinical decision-making, Received 21 May 2025 including patient screening, diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring Accepted as revised 4 September 2025 therapeutic responses. Therefore, laboratory errors can significantly impact Available online 11 September 2025 patient care and outcomes. Keywords: Objectives: To identify and quantify the types and frequencies of errors in the Laboratory error, laboratory testing total testing process of the medical laboratory department, with the goal of process, pre-analytical phase. reducing preventable errors and improving overall quality. Materials and methods: This retrospective descriptive study analyzed error records, incident reports and nonconformities from January 2021, to December, 2023. Errors were categorized by testing phase: pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical. Specimen sources were classified as outpatient, inpatient, or external (outside hospital). Data were summarized using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages and Six Sigma performance scale values. Results: A total of 2,261,729 specimens were received during the study period. The overall error rate was 0.197% (4,460 errors). Error rates by phase were 0.116% for pre-analytical, 0.077% for analytical, and 0.004% for post- analytical. Six Sigma performance scores were 4.60 (pre-analytical), 4.70 (analytical), and 5.50 (post-analytical), all within acceptable quality thresholds (>4.15, >3.85 and >4.80, respectively). The most common pre-analytical error was clotted samples (1,233 cases). Analytical errors were dominated by unacceptable internal quality control results (1,088 cases). The most frequent post-analytical error was excessive turnaround time (54 cases). Pre-analytical errors occurred most frequently in inpatient specimens (76.90%), with clotted samples accounting for 41.49% of those cases. Six Sigma values by specimen source were 4.20 for inpatients, 4.90 for outpatients and 4.90 for external sources. Conclusion: Most laboratory errors occurred in the pre-analytical phase, primarily due to specimen collection issues related to quality and volume, particularly in the inpatient setting. Targeted preventative measures-especially in pre-analytical processes-are essential to minimize errors and improve patient safety. Analytical errors were primarily due to unacceptable IQC, EQA. JSON: Name: preanalytical_sigma_intervention Title: Prospective cluster-randomized intervention trial combining targeted pre-analytical phlebotomy training and sigma-metrics-guided quality control to reduce laboratory testing errors in a tertiary hospital medical laboratory Short Hypothesis: Implementing a combined intervention of targeted pre-analytical phlebotomy training and sigma-metrics-guided quality control will reduce the pre-analytical error rate by at least 30% relative to baseline within 12 months. Related Work: Retrospective analyses across multiple laboratories consistently identify the pre-analytical phase as the largest contributor to total testing errors and use Six Sigma metrics to quantify process quality. Prior work has applied Six Sigma and Westgard approaches primarily as assessment tools rather than as part of prospective, controlled interventions. Studies report high variability in reported error rates due to heterogeneous error definitions, manual documentation, and lack of standardized, ward-level stratification. Existing interventions are typically single-component (phlebotomy training or IT integration) and measured without concurrent controls or randomized designs. Quality Goal Index (QGI) and risk-matrix approaches have been proposed to prioritize corrective action but have seldom been combined with systematic staff training and real-time error reporting. Limitations in current methods include retrospective designs, underreporting bias, absence of cluster-randomized evaluation, insufficient sample-size planning given low baseline error rates, and lack of ablation studies to separate effects of training, QC-rule selection, and LIS integration. Abstract: Problem: Pre-analytical specimen collection errors dominate laboratory testing errors and drive recollection, delays, and diagnostic risk. Approach: Conduct a prospective cluster-randomized trial in a tertiary hospital laboratory to evaluate a combined intervention composed of structured pre-analytical phlebotomy training, sigma-metrics-guided selection of quality-control rules (including QGI stratification), and enhanced error reporting via a cloud-based HRMS. Main contribution: Provide the first randomized, ward-level quantification of intervention effects on phase-specific error rates with direct comparison among full intervention, training-only, QC-only, and control arms, and present ablation data isolating the incremental value of LIS/HIS integration. Expected outcome: Demonstration of a clinically meaningful reduction in pre-analytical errors (target ≥30% relative reduction), improved Six Sigma performance and QGI profiles, and evidence on which components (training, sigma-driven QC, IT integration) yield the largest marginal impact on error reduction and turnaround time. Experiments: Design: Cluster-randomized trial with four arms applied at ward/collection-unit level (full intervention = training + sigma-driven QC + HRMS/LIS integration; training-only; sigma-driven QC-only; control) using a stepped-wedge rollout over 12 months. Retrospective baseline dataset: three-year historical records (January 2021–December 2023) with 2,261,729 specimens and phase-classified errors. Prospective dataset: 12 months following intervention rollout, target >=750,000 specimens (approx. baseline annual throughput). Inclusion/exclusion: same as baseline study; exclude non-test administrative errors. Error classification: pre-analytical, analytical, post-analytical per predefined taxonomy; use automated HRMS tagging plus manual adjudication for ambiguous cases. Baselines for comparison: (1) historical baseline (aggregate 2021–2023 rates), (2) concurrent control clusters. Evaluation metrics: primary outcome = pre-analytical error rate (errors/specimens); secondary outcomes = analytical and post-analytical error rates, Six Sigma values per phase (Westgard calculator), QGI per analyte, median and 90th percentile turnaround time, recollection rate, number of IQC/EQA failures, cost per recollection. Statistical analysis: compare proportions via cluster-adjusted chi-square and mixed-effects Poisson regression with random intercepts for clusters and fixed effects for time periods; interrupted time-series analysis for temporal trends; pre-specified subgroup analyses by specimen source (inpatient/outpatient/external) and ward type. Power/sample size: to detect a 30% relative reduction in pre-analytical error rate from 0.116% to 0.081% with alpha=0.05 and power=0.8 requires ~130,000 specimens per arm (approximate); therefore plan enrollment targets accordingly. Comparison/ablation: compare full intervention vs training-only vs QC-only vs control; additional ablation: within full-intervention clusters, toggle HRMS/LIS integration to quantify marginal effect of automated reporting; report effect sizes, 95% CIs, and p-values. Data processing: compute Six Sigma and QGI per analyte monthly, produce dashboards for monitoring but keep dashboards passive for control arm. Significance threshold p<0.05, adjust for multiple secondary outcomes using false discovery rate. Risk Factors and Limitations: Low baseline error rates create statistical power challenges and require large specimen volumes per arm; residual underreporting or misclassification of errors may bias effect estimates; Hawthorne effect may transiently reduce errors in all clusters irrespective of intervention; cluster-level confounding (differences in staff experience, patient mix, or ward workflow) may limit causal attribution despite randomization; implementation fidelity may vary across clusters (inconsistent training uptake or QC-rule adherence); reliance on new HRMS/LIS integration introduces operational risks such as downtime, data-sync errors, and privacy compliance constraints; generalizability may be limited to similar tertiary, accredited laboratories with comparable automation and sample volumes; measuring impact on patient-level clinical outcomes is out of scope and limits demonstration of downstream clinical benefit; computing and analysis require robust infrastructure for near-real-time Six Sigma and QGI calculations, which may limit scalability in resource-limited settings.
